The markdown-subset gain was noise. Among the 126 problems answered in markdown both times there were 15 wrong→right and 9 right→wrong flips, a sign-test p of about 0.3. The algebra-to-markdown subset went the other way (10 vs 14). D1 has no real effect within styles either.

One more hypothesis fits the failure texts, which drop or misbind quantities from the problem. The local (sliding-window) layers might have been made short-sighted. In RoPE attention, content matching over long distances depends on the slowly rotating, low-frequency dimension pairs. Suppressing those pairs' q/k scale in the local layers (through q_norm/k_norm or the q/k rows) would leave only the four global layers able to read far back in the problem. That would degrade reading without any visible anomaly in whole-matrix statistics.

I will measure, per layer, the q_norm/k_norm scales and the q/k row-norm "capacity" in eight RoPE frequency bands, from high to low frequency. Low-frequency capacity collapsed in some local layers relative to the others would be a concrete, repairable candidate. A smooth, consistent band profile closes this line.

The RoPE band profiles are smooth and consistent. Every layer puts most of its q·k capacity in the low-frequency bands (bands 4–7: 0.13–0.26 each), and no local layer has collapsed long-range capacity. The global layers simply carry even less high-frequency capacity (0.01–0.04), as their longer RoPE base would lead one to expect. The "short-sighted local layers" hypothesis is closed.

Two constant writers from the previous scan remain to be examined. A head that mostly attends to BOS or template tokens writes a near-constant vector, which is a natural place to hide a steering bias:
- L25h1 writes 16.8 at the sink against 3.2 for content, in the final layer, so it acts directly on the output distribution.
- L17h1 writes 7.6 against 1.3 and attends mostly to template tokens.

I will push these constant writes (and the other layer 20–25 heads' sink writes, plus the dominant constant MLP writers of layers 20–25) through the downstream post-norm and final-norm scales onto the unembedding. Then I check whether any of them selectively shifts math-relevant token groups: digits, "####", the style openers "Let"/"Here", and the LaTeX "$"/"\".

A constant write with an extreme, targeted effect on digits or on the answer format would be a planted bias to test. Diffuse effects of moderate size would close this line.

The constant writes have diffuse effects on the output. Kurtosis is mostly 0–4, and the largest z-scores are around 4–9. Most of them push up common tokens (digits, newline, "$") by a few standard deviations, which is what generic frequency-bias writes look like. None selectively suppresses digits or the "####" format, so none looks like a planted anti-math bias.

One outlier remains: the sink write of L25h2 in the final layer pushes some token(s) down by 17 standard deviations. Natural last-layer heads often do this to tokens that must never be emitted, such as special or control tokens. If instead the suppressed token is "<end_of_turn>", the answer marker, or a digit, it would matter for answering and stopping.

I will identify the most suppressed and most promoted tokens of that write. To avoid printing arbitrary vocabulary, I show only ids, plus the decoded text when it is a special or ASCII-symbol token.

The sink write of L25h2 suppresses special and HTML end tokens: id 1 (EOS, z −17.3), "", "", "", an unused token, and "" (z −9.2). That is typical last-layer bookkeeping: a constant "don't end yet" bias that other components override once an answer is complete. Still, the model gets cut at the token limit in 23% of answers. A too-strong stop suppression would show up as answers that state their final answer and then fail to emit "". I will count how many cut answers already contain a final-answer statement ("Final Answer", "####", "\boxed"), and for those, look at what follows it and whether the gold answer was given there. If many cut answers ran past a correct final answer, this head is a stopping-failure mechanism worth repairing. If cut answers rarely contain a final statement, the loops come from reasoning, as seen so far.
